exercise-library: Tap Chest, Back, Shoulders, Arms, Legs and glutes, Core, Cardio, Stretching or Yoga, or leave it on All to scroll through every group on one page.
Filter by equipment (none, dumbbell, barbell, machine or bands, kettlebell and ball) and by level, or search for an exercise or a muscle such as squat or biceps.
Each picture fades between the start and the end position so you can see the movement. Open "How to do it" for the steps.
Choose one or two exercises per area, warm up first and finish with a stretch. Start light and stop if anything hurts.
workout-planner: Build a workout or start from a quick plan

Tap 5, 10, 15, 20 or 30 minutes with or without equipment and the planner fills a warm-up, a main part and a cool-down to fit the time. Or tap a quick plan such as Push day, Home, Morning yoga or Evening wind-down, or start empty and build your own.

Add exercises from the list, move them up or down, change the note on each one, or remove them. If an exercise is not in the list, add it with your own name and a note. It shows as text without a picture.
Set the date, workout name, gym name, seconds per exercise and rest. Switch pictures, muscles, steps, countdown and next exercise on or off.
Tap Start slideshow for one big exercise at a time, or Show all on one screen to see warm-up, main and cool-down together with small pictures and a timer on each exercise.
weekly-workout-plans: Tap Gym for barbells, dumbbells and machines, At home for body weight and a pair of dumbbells, or Yoga for poses and stretches with no equipment.
Three days is full body each time and suits beginners. Four days splits upper and lower body. Five days gives one muscle area a day plus a lighter day. The days to train on are shown under the title.
Open a day and look at the moves

Each day lists a warm-up, the main moves and a cool-down, each with a picture, the muscles it works and the sets and reps or the hold time. The plan is fixed, so you can follow the same week again and again.
Choose Show this day on a screen to open it in the Workout Planner with timers and pictures, or copy the day or the whole week as text for a chat or a note.
one-rep-max-and-plate-calculator: Type the weight you lifted and the reps you completed with good form. Sets of 2 to 10 reps give the most reliable estimate.
The tool averages the Epley and Brzycki formulas and shows your estimated one-rep max, with each formula alongside.
The table lists the weight at 100, 95, 90 percent and lower, the reps you can usually do at that weight and the plates needed on each side of the bar.
In the plate calculator, type the weight on the bar, choose your bar and the tool lists the plates for each side, heaviest first.
running-pace-calculator: Pick Find my pace, Find my finish time or Find the distance, and choose kilometres or miles.
Enter the distance and your time, or your distance and pace, depending on the mode. Tap 5K, 10K, half marathon or marathon to fill in a common distance.
See your pace per kilometre or mile, finish time, distance and speed in kilometres or miles an hour.
Check the split table for a time at every kilometre or mile, and the predicted race times for other distances based on your run.
workout-log: Choose the day, then type part of an exercise name and pick it from the list of more than 300 exercises, stretches and yoga poses.
Type each set as weight x reps, separated by commas, for example 60x8, 60x8, 65x6. For body weight moves use 0 as the weight.
Tap Save to my log. It is saved on your device straight away and appears in your history.
Each exercise gets a progress line based on your best set each day, and a New best label when you beat your earlier days.

fitnessExerciseLibrary.title: Exercise Library
fitnessExerciseLibrary.subtitle: Browse gym and home exercises by body area, with moving pictures and step-by-step instructions. Filter by equipment and level. Free, no sign-up.
faq: Where do the pictures and instructions come from?

They come from the free-exercise-db project, an open dataset released into the public domain. Each exercise has a photo of the start position and a photo of the end position. This page fades between the two so the movement is easy to follow. We chose 318 common exercises and stretches from the larger dataset. The 21 yoga poses are different: their pictures are our own line drawings, four for each pose, that move from the start into the hold and back.
Is this medical advice? Are these exercises right for me?

No. This is general information and not medical advice. If you are injured, pregnant, recovering from surgery, have a heart, joint or blood-pressure condition, or have not exercised for a long time, talk to a doctor or a qualified trainer before you start. Begin with a light weight, keep good form and stop if you feel sharp pain, dizziness or chest discomfort.
How many sets and reps should I do?

It depends on your goal and level. Many beginners start with two or three sets of eight to twelve repetitions, using a weight that makes the last few repetitions hard while keeping good form. Lower repetitions with heavier weights build strength, and higher repetitions with lighter weights build muscular endurance. A trainer can set numbers for your body and goals.
How often should I train each muscle?

A common guideline is to train each major muscle group about two times a week and to leave a day or two of rest before working the same muscles hard again. Spread your sessions across the week, for example upper body, lower body and core on different days, or a full body session on alternate days.
Can I use this at home without a gym?

Yes. Set the equipment filter to No equipment for bodyweight exercises such as push-ups, squats, lunges, planks and bridges, or to Dumbbell if you own a pair. The Stretching group needs no equipment either.
What is the difference between the Cardio and the strength groups?

Cardio exercises keep your heart rate raised for a longer time, for example cycling, rowing, jogging, skipping or jumping moves. Strength exercises work muscles against resistance, in short sets with rests in between. A balanced week usually includes both, plus stretching.
Is my information uploaded or stored?
No. Searching and filtering happen in your browser and nothing you type is sent to {{siteName}}. The page still loads the exercise pictures, advertising and other resources from the network.

fitnessWorkoutPlanner.title: Workout Planner and Gym Display
fitnessWorkoutPlanner.subtitle: Plan today’s warm-up, main workout and cool-down, add your own exercises, and show them as a slideshow or all on one screen with pictures and timers. Free.
faq: Can I use an exercise that is not in the list?

Yes. Every part (warm-up, main workout and cool-down) has an Add your own form. Type a name and a note, such as a reason or a count, and it joins the plan. It shows on the slideshow as text, because there is no picture for it.
When does a picture show on the slideshow?
Only for exercises picked from the list, which has two pictures for each. Your own entries show the name and note without a picture. You can also switch pictures off for every slide.
What are the quick starts?

Ready plans such as Mix day, Push day, Pull day, Leg day, Full body, Home, Cardio and core, Morning yoga and Evening wind-down. Tap one to fill all three parts, then change anything. Build me a workout is different: you choose the time, the equipment, the focus and the level, and it picks the moves. Undo brings back what you had before.
Can I show it on a gym TV or a phone?

Yes. Open the page on the screen you want, build or load the plan and choose Start slideshow for one exercise at a time, or Show all on one screen for the whole plan at once. Both go fullscreen where the browser allows it and try to keep the screen awake. Press Escape or Close to leave.
What does the one-screen view show?

The three parts side by side, each exercise with a small picture (library exercises only), your note and a time button. Tap the time to count down, tap the circle to tick an exercise off, and use the session clock for the whole workout. There are no long descriptions, so it all fits on one screen.
Is this medical advice? Is the plan right for me?

No. This is general information and not medical advice. If you are injured, pregnant, recovering, have a heart, joint or blood-pressure condition, or have not exercised for a long time, talk to a doctor or a qualified trainer first. Start light and stop if something hurts.
Is my plan uploaded or stored?

No. The plan stays in your browser, saved on this device only, and nothing you type is sent to {{siteName}}. The page still loads the exercise pictures, advertising and other resources from the network.

fitnessWeeklyPlans.title: Weekly Workout Plans: Fixed 3, 4 and 5 Day Gym, Home and Yoga Routines
fitnessWeeklyPlans.subtitle: Fixed weekly plans for the gym, home or yoga. Pick 3, 4 or 5 days and every main muscle is covered, with a picture for every move. Free, no sign-up.
faq: Why are these plans fixed and not random?

A routine only works when you can repeat it and add a little weight or a few reps over the weeks. If the moves changed every day you could not tell whether you were improving. These plans stay the same, so you learn the moves and can see your progress.
Which plan should I choose, 3, 4 or 5 days?

Choose the number of days you can keep up for months, not the biggest number. Three full-body days suit beginners and busy weeks. Four days with two upper and two lower body days train each muscle twice a week. Five days gives each muscle area its own day, plus a lighter full-body day.
Do the plans cover every muscle?

Yes. The gym and home plans train the chest, upper back, lats, lower back, shoulders, biceps, triceps, quads, hamstrings, glutes, calves and abs across the week. We checked this against the muscles listed for every move in the Exercise Library. The yoga plans work the whole body, with a mix of legs, core, back and hips.
What does the home plan need?

Your body weight and a pair of dumbbells. A few muscles, such as the biceps and calves, are hard to train without any weight, so those moves use the dumbbells. Each move shows the equipment it needs, so you can swap or skip it.
Can I show a day on a gym or class screen?

Yes. Open a day and choose Show this day on a screen. The Workout Planner opens with that day filled in, and you can start the slideshow with pictures and timers or show the whole day on one screen. It replaces the plan saved in the planner, so copy it first if you want to keep the old one.
Are these plans medical advice?

No. They are general fitness routines, not advice for your body or any health condition. Start light, keep good form, stop if anything hurts and talk to a doctor first if you have an injury, a heart condition, are pregnant or have not exercised for a long time.
Is my choice uploaded or stored?

No. Everything runs in your browser and nothing you choose is sent to {{siteName}}. Opening a day in the Workout Planner saves it on this device only. The page still loads the exercise pictures, advertising and other resources from the network.

fitnessOneRepMax.title: One-Rep Max and Plate Calculator: Estimate Your Max and Load the Bar
fitnessOneRepMax.subtitle: Estimate your one-rep max from any set, see training weights at each percentage and the plates for each side of the bar. Free, in kg or lb, no sign-up.
faq: What is a one-rep max?

It is the heaviest weight you could lift once with good form. Most people never test it directly, because it is hard and risky. Instead they estimate it from a lighter set of several reps, which is what this tool does.
How does the estimate work?

The tool uses two well-known formulas. Epley multiplies your weight by one plus the reps divided by 30. Brzycki multiplies your weight by 36 and divides by 37 minus the reps. The headline number is the average of the two, which is steadier than either alone.
How accurate is it?

It is a good guide, not a promise. The formulas work best for 2 to 10 reps and get less accurate above about 12. They also vary between people and lifts, and they are usually closer for the bench press than for the deadlift or the squat.
What do the percentages and reps mean?

Training plans often say to lift at a share of your max, such as three sets of five at 80 percent. The table does that sum and shows the plates for each weight. The reps column is a rough guide to how many reps people can usually do at that share.
How do I load the bar with the plate calculator?

Enter the total weight you want on the bar and pick your bar. Because both sides must match, the tool takes off the bar weight, halves the rest and picks the biggest plates first. If the plates cannot make the exact weight it shows the closest weight under it.
Is it safe to test a true one-rep max?

A true max is a very hard effort. Only try one with a spotter or safety arms, after a thorough warm-up, and only if you have trained the lift for a while. If you have an injury or a health condition, check with a doctor first. The estimate on this page is a safer way to plan your training.
Is anything I enter uploaded or stored?

No. Everything runs in your browser and nothing you enter is sent to {{siteName}}. Your numbers stay in the page and are not saved. The page still loads fonts, advertising and other resources from the network.

fitnessRunningPace.title: Running Pace Calculator: Pace, Finish Time, Splits and Race Predictions
fitnessRunningPace.subtitle: Work out your running pace, finish time or distance, see splits for every kilometre or mile and predict 5K to marathon times from one run. Free, no sign-up.
faq: How is running pace calculated?

Pace is the time taken divided by the distance covered. A 5 kilometre run in 30 minutes is 6 minutes for each kilometre. The tool also shows the matching speed, which is the distance divided by the time in hours.
Can I work in miles?
Yes. Switch between kilometres and miles and every number follows, including the pace, the speed and the split table. A mile is 1.609344 kilometres.
What are split times for?
Splits show the time you should reach at each kilometre or mile if you hold an even pace. Many runners write them on a band or a phone note to check they are on target during a race.
How are race times predicted?

The tool uses the Riegel formula, which multiplies your time by the ratio of the two distances raised to the power 1.06. It works best for runs between about 1.5 kilometres and a marathon and when you have trained for the longer distance.
How accurate are the predictions?

They are a guide. They assume a hard, well-paced effort and enough training for the new distance. For the half marathon and marathon, many runners find real results slower than the prediction because stamina and fuelling matter more over long races.
How do I convert a treadmill speed to a pace?
Use Find my pace with a distance of 1 kilometre or mile and the time that speed takes, or use Find my finish time and enter the pace. As a check, 10 kilometres an hour is 6 minutes a kilometre.
Is anything I enter uploaded or stored?
No. Everything runs in your browser and nothing you enter is sent to {{siteName}}. Your times are used only in the page. The page still loads fonts, advertising and other resources from the network.

fitnessWorkoutLog.title: Workout Log: Track Sets, Reps and Weights, See Your Progress
fitnessWorkoutLog.subtitle: Log your sets, reps and weights from more than 300 exercises, see progress charts and new bests. Saved on your device with no account and no sign-up.
faq: How do I write my sets?

Write each set as the weight, an x and the reps, such as 60x8. Separate sets with commas, so 60x8, 60x8, 65x6 is three sets. For body weight moves such as push-ups, write 0 for the weight, such as 0x15.
How is progress measured?

For weighted moves the tool takes your best set each day, works out an estimated one-rep max from it and plots one point a day. For body weight moves it uses your most reps. A rising line means you are getting stronger.
What does New best mean?
It appears when your latest day beats every earlier day for that exercise. It needs at least two days of data, so you will see it from your second session.
Where is my log kept?

In your browser on this device only. Nothing is sent to a server, so it works without an account, but clearing your browser data or using another browser or phone will not show it. Use Copy my log as CSV now and then to keep a backup.
Can I move my log to a spreadsheet?
Yes. Copy my log as CSV puts the date, exercise and sets on your clipboard. Paste it into Excel or Google Sheets and it fills in columns.
Which weight unit does it use?
Pick kilograms or pounds at the top. The unit only changes how the numbers are labelled, so switch it before you start and keep to one unit.
Is anything I enter uploaded or stored?

No. Everything runs in your browser and nothing you enter is sent to {{siteName}}. Your log is saved only in this browser on this device. The page still loads fonts, advertising and other resources from the network.

sections.heading: What the library covers
paragraphs: The library lists 339 exercises, stretches and yoga poses in nine groups: chest, back, shoulders, arms, legs and glutes, core, cardio, stretching and yoga. For every exercise you see the muscles it mainly works, the muscles that help, the equipment it needs, a level from beginner to advanced and numbered steps.

Each picture shows two positions and fades between them in a loop, so you can see the start, the movement and the finish without playing a video. If your device is set to reduce motion, the pictures stay still and show the start position.

sections.heading: Putting a balanced session together
paragraphs: A simple full body session picks one exercise from each of a few areas: a press for the chest or shoulders, a pull for the back, a squat or lunge for the legs, and one core exercise. Pairing pushing and pulling movements keeps the shoulders balanced, and finishing with core work and a short stretch rounds off the session.
If you train at home, filter by No equipment first and add a pair of dumbbells later. If you use a gym, machines and cables are a gentle way to learn a movement before you move to free weights.

sections.heading: Warming up and cooling down
paragraphs: Spend five to ten minutes before lifting on easy cardio such as cycling or brisk walking, and on a few mobility moves from the Stretching group, such as arm circles and hip circles. After training, slower stretches for the muscles you used help you wind down.
Stretching does not replace rest. Sleep, enough food and a day or two between hard sessions for the same muscles matter as much as the exercises themselves.

sections.heading: Staying safe
paragraphs: Good form matters more than heavy weight. Learn each movement with a light weight or none at all, control the weight on the way down, and breathe steadily instead of holding your breath. Ask a trainer to check your form on the big lifts such as squats and deadlifts.

Stop and rest if you feel sharp pain, dizziness or chest discomfort, and speak to a doctor about it. The photos and steps come from an open dataset, so they are a starting point and not a replacement for personal coaching.

sections.heading: One plan for the whole session
paragraphs: A good session has three parts: a warm-up that raises your heart rate and loosens the joints, a main workout with cardio or muscle exercises, and a cool-down with slower stretches. The planner keeps these as three separate lists so nothing is forgotten.

Pick a quick start for a day type such as push, pull, legs or a mix, then adjust it. You can reorder exercises, rename the plan and add a short note to each exercise, for example a count or a reason for a swap.

sections.heading: Your own exercises are welcome
paragraphs: The list holds more than 300 exercises, stretches and yoga poses with two pictures each, but every gym has machines and moves that are not in it. Each part has an Add your own form for a name and a note.
Your entries sit in the plan next to the others. They show on the slideshow without a picture, so the screen stays honest about what it has.

sections.heading: Showing it on a screen
paragraphs: The slideshow shows one exercise at a time with the date, the plan name and, if you want, the muscles, the steps and a countdown. The one-screen view shows the whole plan at once with small pictures, a timer on each exercise and a session clock, which suits a gym wall TV. Both work on a phone on a stand too.
This page gives general information and not medical advice. Keep a light start, good form and a rest day between hard sessions for the same muscles, and stop if something hurts.

sections.heading: A fixed plan you can repeat
paragraphs: Most people stop going to the gym because they never know what to do next. A fixed weekly plan answers that. You open the page, pick the number of days you can train, and the same warm-up, main moves and cool-down are waiting every week. Because the moves do not change, you can add a little weight or a rep each week and see yourself improve.

There are nine plans: 3, 4 and 5 days, each for the gym, for home and for yoga. Every plan lists the days of the week to train so the rest days fall in the right place, and every move has a picture, the muscles it works and the sets and reps or the hold time.

sections.heading: How the days are split
paragraphs: Three days a week uses full-body sessions on alternate days. Each session trains legs, chest, back, shoulders, arms and core, with different moves on each day so no muscle gets bored. Four days splits the week into two upper-body days and two lower-body days, so every muscle is trained twice. Five days gives the chest and triceps, back and biceps, legs and glutes, and shoulders and core a day each, and ends with a lighter full-body and cardio day.

The gym and home plans were checked move by move against the muscles each exercise works, so the chest, back, shoulders, arms, legs, glutes, calves and abs are all trained in every plan. The yoga plans follow a similar rhythm: a flow, a strength and balance day, a hips and hamstrings day and a slow evening stretch.

sections.heading: Using the plans well
paragraphs: Start with the plan that has fewer days than you think you can manage. A plan you finish is better than a bigger plan you drop. Begin with weights you can lift with good form, stop a rep or two before you are exhausted and add a little each week. On rest days a walk or gentle stretching is enough.

Choose Show this day on a screen to open any day in the Workout Planner, where you can run it as a slideshow with timers on a phone, a gym TV or a class screen. These are general routines and not medical advice, so check with a doctor first if you have an injury or a health condition.

sections.heading: Estimating a max without testing it
paragraphs: Your one-rep max is the starting point for most strength plans, because training weights are often written as a share of it. Testing a true max is hard on the body and carries a risk of injury, so most people estimate it from a set of a few reps. Lift a weight as many times as you can with good form, enter the weight and the reps, and the calculator does the rest.

Two formulas are used because each has a weakness. Epley can run a little high for low reps and Brzycki rises quickly as the reps climb. Averaging them gives a steadier figure. The estimate is most trustworthy for sets of 2 to 10 reps, and for longer sets it is better to treat the number as a ballpark.

sections.heading: Using percentages in training
paragraphs: Many programs ask for work at a set share of your max, such as 70 percent for sets of eight or 85 percent for sets of three. The table on this page turns your max into the actual weights, so you do not have to work them out in the gym. The usual reps beside each share are a rough guide, since a lighter lift such as a curl lets most people do more reps at a given percentage than a heavy leg lift does.
Re-test your estimate every few weeks. As you get stronger your max rises and the weights in the table go up with it. You can keep track of your sets over time in the Workout Log tool.

sections.heading: Loading the barbell
paragraphs: A barbell is loaded evenly on both sides, so the plate calculator subtracts the weight of the bar, splits what is left and lists the plates for one side, heaviest first. Choose the bar you use, whether a standard bar, a lighter women's bar or a short bar, because the bar weight changes the sum.

Always use collars to hold the plates in place. If your gym has different plates than the ones listed, such as 20 pound plates or 1 kilogram plates, you can still use the plate list as a starting point and adjust it by hand.

sections.heading: Pace, speed and time
paragraphs: Runners talk about pace, which is the time for each kilometre or mile, while treadmills and watches often show speed. They describe the same thing in different ways. The calculator converts between them, so a 5:30 pace per kilometre becomes about 10.9 kilometres an hour, and you can see both on the screen at once.

The three modes cover the questions runners ask most. Find my pace answers what pace they ran. Find my finish time shows what time a target pace gives over a race distance. Find the distance shows how far you will go in a set time at a steady pace, which is handy for timed runs.

sections.heading: Splits and pacing
paragraphs: An even pace is the safest plan for most races, and splits turn your goal into checkpoints. The table lists the time you should reach at each kilometre or mile, with a final line for the finish if the distance is not a whole number. Going out too fast and fading is the most common pacing mistake, so keep the first few splits close to the plan.
Copy the summary to share your result or paste it into a training log, and print or save the page as a PDF if you want to carry the splits with you.

sections.heading: Predicting other race distances
paragraphs: If you have just run a hard 5K, you can estimate what a 10K or a half marathon might look like. The Riegel formula behind the predictions is simple and well known, but it assumes you will train properly for the longer race. Treat the numbers as a target to build towards and not a guarantee.

Use the predictions to set sensible goals, not to choose a pace on race day. Weather, hills, sleep and fuelling all change how a race goes, and a comfortable start almost always gives the best finish.

sections.heading: Why keep a log
paragraphs: Getting stronger depends on doing a little more over time, whether it is an extra rep, a few more kilograms or an extra set. That is easy to say and hard to remember without a record. A log takes the guessing out: you can see what you lifted last time and aim to beat it.
This log is made to be quick enough to use between sets. You type the date, find the exercise, write the sets in a short line and save. There is no account, no sign-up and nothing to install.

sections.heading: Reading your progress
paragraphs: For each exercise the tool picks your best set on each day and turns it into an estimated one-rep max, so a heavy set of three can be compared fairly with a lighter set of ten. The chart shows how that number changes from session to session, and a New best label appears when you beat your earlier days.
Do not worry if the line wobbles. Sleep, food and stress change how a session goes, so look at the trend over a few weeks and not at a single day.

sections.heading: Keeping your data safe
paragraphs: Your log is stored only in your browser on this device. That keeps it private, but it also means it can be lost if you clear your site data or change phone. The Copy my log as CSV button puts everything on your clipboard so you can paste it into a spreadsheet as a backup.
The log works well with the fixed plans in Weekly Workout Plans. Follow a plan, log each session and watch the numbers go up.
